figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: EGFR kinase active site—hinge hydrogen bond geometry exploited by all approved EGFR inhibitors.

key_facts: EGFR kinase domain solved at 2.6 Å by Stamos, Sliwkowski, and Eigenbrot at Genentech, published in J. Biol. Chem. in 2002.
EGFR exon 19 deletions and L858R are driver oncogene alterations in 10-15% of Western and 30-40% of East Asian lung adenocarcinomas.
Erlotinib and gefitinib bind the ATP pocket via a hydrogen bond to hinge Met769.
T790M gatekeeper mutation is the primary mechanism of acquired resistance to first- and second-generation EGFR inhibitors.
Osimertinib, a covalent third-generation inhibitor, achieves >80% response rate in T790M-positive tumors.
EGFR is overexpressed or mutated in lung, colorectal, head and neck, and pancreatic cancers.
EGFR therapy is the founding example of personalized oncology: match mutation to drug.
significance: EGFR kinase proved the concept of oncogene-targeted therapy: identify the driving mutation, solve the structure, design an inhibitor, treat only patients with that mutation. This framework has been applied to over 30 additional kinase targets and transformed lung cancer from uniformly fatal to a condition where many patients achieve years of disease control.

name: CYP3A4
title: The Great Metabolizer: CYP3A4 and the Chemistry of Drug Fate
abstract: Cytochrome P450 3A4 is the single enzyme responsible for metabolizing approximately 50% of all clinically used drugs. Jed Yano and colleagues solved the human CYP3A4 structure at 2.05 Å in 2004, finally explaining how one active site could accommodate substrates ranging from tiny steroids to large macrolide antibiotics.

sections.content: One Enzyme to Metabolize Them All

In 2004, Jed K. Yano, Manika Wester, Gian Schoch, Kerry J. Griffin, C. David Stout, and Eric F. Johnson solved the crystal structure of human CYP3A4 at 2.05 Å and published it in the Journal of Biological Chemistry. CYP3A4 is a microsomal cytochrome P450 that uses a heme iron center and molecular oxygen to oxidize an extraordinary range of substrates—steroids, macrolides, benzodiazepines, statins, immunosuppressants.
See Fig. 1
A Cavernous Active Site

The CYP3A4 active site volume (~1,385 cubic angstroms) is among the largest of any human drug-metabolizing enzyme. Flexible peripheral helices (F, F', G', and G) can expand to accommodate macrolide antibiotics like erythromycin (MW 734 Da) or contract around smaller steroids. This plasticity is the structural explanation for CYP3A4's broad substrate promiscuity.
See Fig. 2
Drug Interactions and Clinical Consequences

CYP3A4 inhibitors (grapefruit furanocoumarins, ketoconazole, ritonavir) can raise co-administered drug plasma levels to toxic concentrations. Inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine) reduce drug levels to subtherapeutic concentrations. Over 200 clinically significant CYP3A4 drug-drug interactions are listed in the FDA's database.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of CYP3A4 showing the classical P450 fold: alpha-helical core (red) with the heme prosthetic group (sticks) at the catalytic center. The flexible F-G loop that expands for large substrates is shown in orange.
Molecular surface of CYP3A4 sliced to reveal the cavernous substrate-binding pocket above the heme iron.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Human CYP3A4 (2HI4) at 2.05 Å—the largest active site of any major human drug-metabolizing P450, capable of simultaneously binding two molecules of erythromycin.

panels.caption: Active site of CYP3A4 showing the heme iron (orange sphere), Cys442 axial ligand, and Thr309 in the I-helix that assists in oxygen activation.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: CYP3A4 active site—heme iron activates molecular oxygen to form compound I (iron-oxo species) which inserts oxygen into C-H bonds.

key_facts: CYP3A4 metabolizes approximately 50% of all clinically prescribed drugs.
The 2.05 Å structure was solved by Yano et al. and published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 2004.
CYP3A4's active site volume (~1,385 cubic angstroms) can simultaneously accommodate two substrate molecules.
The enzyme is expressed primarily in the liver (30% of total P450) and small intestine (70% of intestinal P450).
Grapefruit furanocoumarins (bergamottin, DHB) are mechanism-based irreversible CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Ritonavir is now used as a CYP3A4 inhibitor pharmacoenhancer to increase exposure of co-administered antivirals.
Over 200 clinically significant CYP3A4 drug-drug interactions are listed in the FDA's drug interaction database.
significance: The CYP3A4 structure explained why this single enzyme dominates drug metabolism and provided a structural foundation for predicting and avoiding dangerous drug-drug interactions. The structure is now a required component of regulatory submissions for new drugs.

name: PD-L1
title: The Immune Checkpoint: PD-L1 and the Immunotherapy Revolution
abstract: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) suppresses T-cell activity by binding the PD-1 receptor, allowing tumors to evade immune destruction. Krzysztof Zak and colleagues solved the structure of PD-L1 in complex with a small-molecule inhibitor at 2.2 Å in 2016, revealing an unexpected dimerization mechanism. Antibodies targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis earned James Allison and Tasuku Honjo the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

sections.content: How Tumors Hide from the Immune System

In 2016, Krzysztof Zak, Bogdan Grudnik, Katarzyna Guzik, and colleagues at the Jagiellonian University and Selvita solved the 2.2 Å crystal structure of human PD-L1 bound to BMS-202 and published it in Structure. PD-L1 is expressed on tumor cells and antigen-presenting cells; its binding to PD-1 on T cells delivers an inhibitory signal that halts the immune response.
See Fig. 1
Small Molecules Force a Dimer

The Zak structure revealed that small-molecule PD-L1 inhibitors force two PD-L1 monomers into a face-to-face dimer, burying the PD-1 binding surface. This dimerization mechanism was entirely unexpected and represents a novel mode of inhibition distinct from antibody blockade, opening a pathway to oral PD-L1 inhibitors.
See Fig. 2
Nobel Prize and the Immunotherapy Era

The 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to James P. Allison (anti-CTLA-4) and Tasuku Honjo (PD-1 discovery). Pembrolizumab and atezolizumab are now approved across 20+ cancer indications. Five-year survival in previously fatal metastatic melanoma has improved from under 5% to over 30%.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of the PD-L1 dimer induced by BMS-202. Two PD-L1 monomers (cyan and magenta) arranged face-to-face with the small molecule (yellow sticks) at the dimer interface.
Electrostatic surface of PD-L1 dimer showing the hydrophobic dimerization interface occupied by the inhibitor. The PD-1 binding face is completely occluded.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: PD-L1 inhibitor complex (5C4X) at 2.2 Å—small molecules induce an unexpected face-to-face dimer blocking the PD-1 interaction surface.

panels.caption: PD-L1 dimerization interface showing BMS-202 (yellow) making hydrophobic contacts with Tyr56, Met115, Ala121, and Tyr123 from both monomers.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: The PD-L1 small-molecule binding site at the dimer interface—template for oral immunotherapy drugs.

key_facts: PD-L1 binds PD-1 on T cells to deliver an inhibitory signal—the dominant immune evasion mechanism in solid tumors.
The 2.2 Å complex structure was solved by Zak, Grudnik, Guzik et al. at Jagiellonian University and published in Structure in 2016.
Small-molecule inhibitors induce PD-L1 dimerization, burying the PD-1 binding surface—distinct from therapeutic antibody mechanism.
Pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) and atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) are approved across 20+ cancer indications.
The 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to James Allison and Tasuku Honjo.
Five-year survival in metastatic melanoma improved from <5% to >30% with checkpoint blockade.
Tumor PD-L1 expression (IHC 22C3) is a regulatory biomarker for pembrolizumab monotherapy in lung cancer.
significance: The PD-L1 structure provided the molecular rationale for one of medicine's most transformative advances: immune checkpoint therapy. By revealing how tumors commandeer normal immune suppression, and how inhibitors can physically block that interface, structural biology directly enabled immunotherapies that have extended life for hundreds of thousands of patients with previously incurable cancers.

name: Beta-2 Adrenergic Receptor
title: The Nobel GPCR: Beta-2 Adrenergic Receptor and the G Protein-Coupled Revolution
abstract: The beta-2 adrenergic receptor (beta2AR) was the first human G protein-coupled receptor to be structurally determined, a landmark achieved by Vadim Cherezov, Daniel Rosenbaum, Brian Kobilka, and colleagues in 2007 at 2.4 Å. GPCRs constitute the largest family of membrane protein drug targets, accounting for roughly 35% of all approved drugs. This work contributed to the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for Robert Lefkowitz and Brian Kobilka.

sections.content: Cracking Open the Most Important Drug Target Family

In 2007, Vadim Cherezov, Daniel M. Rosenbaum, Mark A. Hanson, Soren G. F. Rasmussen, and Brian K. Kobilka published the 2.4 Å crystal structure of the human beta2AR in Science. The structure required engineering the receptor with a T4 lysozyme insertion in the third intracellular loop to enable crystallization—a technical tour de force that solved the crystallization problem for flexible membrane proteins.
See Fig. 1
Seven Helices and a Ligand Pocket

Beta2AR comprises seven transmembrane alpha-helices (TM1-TM7). The orthosteric ligand-binding pocket is in the extracellular half of the helix bundle. Carazolol (partial inverse agonist) was co-crystallized in the binding site, revealing the contacts that determine selectivity among adrenergic receptor subtypes. Key interactions include Asp113 (TM3) and Asn312 (TM7) with the catecholamine amine group.
See Fig. 2
Nobel Prize and the GPCR Structural Era

The 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Robert J. Lefkowitz and Brian K. Kobilka for studies of GPCRs. Since the beta2AR structure, over 100 unique GPCR structures have been solved, enabling structure-based design of drugs for heart failure, asthma, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and type 2 diabetes.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of beta2AR showing the seven transmembrane helices (TM1-TM7, rainbow). Carazolol (yellow sticks) is bound in the orthosteric pocket. The palmitoylated C-terminal helix 8 is visible below TM7.
Side view of beta2AR showing the membrane-embedded transmembrane bundle and the extracellular binding pocket.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Human beta2 adrenergic receptor (2RH1) at 2.4 Å—the first high-resolution human GPCR structure.

panels.caption: Orthosteric binding site showing carazolol (yellow) hydrogen bonding to Asp113 and Asn312, and aromatic contacts with Phe290, Trp286, and Phe193.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: beta2AR ligand-binding pocket—contacts that determine subtype selectivity between beta1 and beta2 adrenergic receptors.

key_facts: Beta2AR was the first human GPCR crystal structure, solved at 2.4 Å by Cherezov, Rosenbaum, Kobilka et al., published in Science in 2007.
GPCRs are the largest membrane protein family (~800 members) and target of ~35% of all FDA-approved drugs.
The T4 lysozyme fusion strategy invented for beta2AR crystallization enabled structure determination of dozens of other GPCRs.
Robert Lefkowitz and Brian Kobilka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for GPCR research.
Beta2AR is targeted by bronchodilators (salbutamol) used by over 300 million asthma patients and beta-blockers for heart failure.
The inactive (carazolol-bound) beta2AR structure combined with the active-state structure (2011) revealed conformational changes coupling ligand binding to G protein activation.
Over 100 unique GPCR structures have been determined, enabling structure-based design across neurological, cardiovascular, and metabolic diseases.
significance: The beta2AR structure broke a 20-year barrier in membrane protein crystallography and opened the entire GPCR superfamily to structural biology. With GPCRs as targets for 35% of all approved drugs, every new GPCR structure has immediate pharmacological implications.

name: KcsA Potassium Channel
title: The Selectivity Filter: KcsA and the Atomic Basis of Ion Channel Discrimination
abstract: The KcsA potassium channel from Streptomyces lividans was the first ion channel to be structurally characterized at atomic resolution. Declan Doyle and Roderick MacKinnon solved the 3.2 Å structure in 1998, revealing the elegantly simple selectivity filter that allows K+ to pass at near-diffusion-limited rates while excluding the smaller Na+ ion. This work earned Roderick MacKinnon the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

sections.content: The Filter That Knows K+ from Na+

In 1998, Declan A. Doyle, Joao Morais Cabral, Richard A. Pfuetzner, Anling Kuo, Jacqueline M. Gulbis, Steven L. Cohen, Brian T. Chait, and Roderick MacKinnon published the 3.2 Å crystal structure of KcsA in Science, solving a 50-year mystery: how can potassium channels pass K+ a thousand times faster than the smaller Na+? The selectivity filter, formed by backbone carbonyls of the TVGYG sequence from all four subunits, fits dehydrated K+ precisely but cannot replace the hydration shell of the smaller Na+.
See Fig. 1
Four Subunits, One Pore

KcsA is a homotetramer; each subunit contributes two transmembrane helices and the pore helix that positions the selectivity filter. Four K+ binding sites (S1-S4) within the selectivity filter are occupied in an alternating pattern (S1+S3 or S2+S4), allowing K+ to hop through in a concerted mechanism achieving near-diffusion-limited conductance.
See Fig. 2
Nobel Prize and Channelopathy Medicine

Roderick MacKinnon received the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for structural studies of ion channels. The KcsA structure is the paradigm for understanding the entire potassium channel family, including HERG (cardiac arrhythmia), Kir channels (Andersen syndrome), and KATP channels (neonatal diabetes). Over 100 inherited channelopathies have been mapped onto KcsA-derived structures.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of KcsA homotetramer viewed from the extracellular side. Four subunits (different colors) form a symmetric pore with the selectivity filter visible as a narrow constriction.
Cross-sectional surface of KcsA showing the ion permeation pathway. The narrow selectivity filter (4 angstrom diameter) is flanked by the large central cavity.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: KcsA potassium channel (1BL8) at 3.2 Å—the tetrameric architecture creates a single central pore with exquisite ion selectivity.

panels.caption: KcsA selectivity filter (TVGYG) showing four K+ binding sites (S1-S4) formed by backbone carbonyl oxygens. Purple spheres represent K+ ions at alternating sites. Filter diameter of ~2.8 Å precisely matches the K+ ionic radius.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: The KcsA selectivity filter—backbone carbonyls replace the water hydration shell of K+ perfectly; geometry is too large for Na+, explaining selectivity without sacrificing conductance rate.

key_facts: KcsA was the first ion channel solved at atomic resolution (3.2 Å), published by Doyle, Cabral, Pfuetzner, MacKinnon et al. in Science in 1998.
The TVGYG selectivity filter uses backbone carbonyls to coordinate dehydrated K+ at four binding sites (S1-S4).
K+ selectivity over Na+ (~1000-fold) arises because the filter geometry perfectly replaces K+ hydration waters but cannot do so for the smaller Na+.
Roderick MacKinnon received the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for structural and mechanistic studies of ion channels.
KcsA is a homotetramer with two transmembrane helices per subunit; inner helices form the gating mechanism.
The cardiac HERG K+ channel, responsible for long QT syndrome, is structurally homologous to KcsA and screened against in all drug safety programs.
KcsA provides templates for understanding 100+ inherited ion channel diseases.
significance: KcsA provided the first atomic explanation of ion selectivity, solving a fundamental biophysical puzzle that had resisted solution for decades. The structure is the template for understanding all potassium channels including cardiac HERG (drug-induced arrhythmia). Every drug with arrhythmia liability is now screened against HERG using structural knowledge derived from KcsA.

name: tRNA-Phe
title: The Adapter Molecule at Atomic Resolution: Yeast tRNA-Phe at 1.93 Å
abstract: Transfer RNA (tRNA) is the molecular adapter that reads the genetic code and delivers amino acids to the ribosome. Hong Shi and Peter Moore at Yale solved the crystal structure of yeast phenylalanine tRNA at 1.93 Å in 2000—the highest-resolution tRNA structure ever determined—revealing the intricate network of tertiary interactions, modified nucleosides, and metal ion binding sites that give tRNA its L-shaped architecture.

sections.content: The Cloverleaf in Three Dimensions

In 2000, Hong Shi and Peter B. Moore at Yale University published the 1.93 Å crystal structure of yeast tRNA-Phe in RNA. The 76-nucleotide molecule folds into the canonical L-shaped tertiary structure: the anticodon loop at one end reads the mRNA codon, while the 3'-CCA aminoacyl acceptor stem at the other end carries phenylalanine to the ribosomal A site.
See Fig. 1
Modified Nucleosides and Tertiary Contacts

tRNA-Phe contains 14 modified nucleosides out of 76 total residues—the highest density of modifications of any RNA. These include pseudouridine, ribothymidine, 7-methylguanosine, and wybutosine adjacent to the anticodon. The 1.93 Å structure revealed the precise geometry of all tertiary base pairs and base triples that zip the D-loop and T-loop together.
See Fig. 2
A Window into the Genetic Code

The yeast tRNA-Phe structure illuminates aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase recognition (the 'second genetic code'), ribosomal A-site accommodation, and translational fidelity. Mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes cause MELAS, MERRF, and other tRNA-opathies. The structural database of tRNA modifications informed design of N1-methylpseudouridine used in COVID-19 mRNA vaccines.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of yeast tRNA-Phe showing the L-shaped tertiary structure. The anticodon stem-loop (bottom) contains the GAA anticodon; the acceptor stem (top right) terminates in the 3'-CCA.
All-atom stick model of tRNA-Phe with modified nucleosides highlighted in orange.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Yeast tRNA-Phe (1EHZ) at 1.93 Å—the highest-resolution tRNA structure. The L-shape positions anticodon and aminoacyl acceptor ~75 Å apart, spanning the ribosomal A site.

panels.caption: Tertiary core showing D-loop/TpsiC-loop interface with base triples and a coordinated Mg2+ ion (green sphere). Modified nucleoside wybutosine (yellow) adjacent to the anticodon is visible.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: Tertiary interactions in yeast tRNA-Phe—D-loop (blue) and TpsiC-loop (red) form an intricate network of base triples and metal ion contacts rigidifying the L-shaped scaffold.

key_facts: Yeast tRNA-Phe solved at 1.93 Å by Hong Shi and Peter Moore at Yale, published in RNA in 2000—the highest resolution tRNA structure.
The 76-nucleotide tRNA adopts an L-shaped fold with anticodon loop and aminoacyl acceptor stem separated by ~75 Å.
tRNA-Phe contains 14 modified nucleosides, the highest density of any RNA, including wybutosine adjacent to the anticodon.
The anticodon GAA reads UUC/UUU phenylalanine codons; the 3'-CCA acceptor terminus carries the charged amino acid.
Mitochondrial tRNA gene mutations cause MELAS, MERRF, and other neuromuscular diseases.
tRNA structural insights informed design of N1-methylpseudouridine in COVID-19 mRNA vaccines to reduce innate immune activation.
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases recognize distinct tRNA features (the 'second genetic code') to ensure correct amino acid assignment.
significance: The 1.93 Å tRNA-Phe structure provided the definitive atomic picture of the genetic code adapter molecule, revealing the complete network of modified nucleosides, metal ions, and tertiary contacts responsible for translational fidelity. This knowledge underpins understanding of mitochondrial disease, antibiotic mechanisms, and the nucleoside modification chemistry central to mRNA vaccine technology.

name: Nucleosome Core Particle
title: Life Packed in a Spool: The Nucleosome Core Particle and Chromatin Architecture
abstract: The nucleosome is the fundamental repeating unit of chromatin, comprising 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped 1.65 turns around an octamer of histone proteins. Karolin Luger, Arno Mader, Robin Richmond, David Sargent, and Timothy Richmond solved the 2.8 Å structure in 1997 at ETH Zurich, revealing the atomic details of DNA-histone recognition and the molecular basis of epigenetic gene regulation.

sections.content: Packing the Genome into a Nucleus

In 1997, Karolin Luger, Arno W. Mader, Robin K. Richmond, David F. Sargent, and Timothy J. Richmond at ETH Zurich published the 2.8 Å crystal structure of the nucleosome core particle in Nature. The structure contained 146 bp of palindromic DNA wrapped 1.65 times around a histone octamer (two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4), explaining how cells compact human chromosomal DNA by a factor of ~10,000.
See Fig. 1
The Histone Octamer and DNA Contacts

The histone octamer is organized as a (H3-H4)2 tetramer flanked by two H2A-H2B dimers. Each histone contains the histone fold domain—a helix-turn-helix motif—and disordered N-terminal tails that protrude from the nucleosome and are sites of post-translational modifications. DNA wraps the octamer with 14 direct contacts per histone pair, primarily at the minor groove, with arginine residues inserting into the minor groove at each DNA bending point.
See Fig. 2
Epigenetics and Disease

The histone tails—sites of acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation—constitute the histone code controlling gene expression. HDAC inhibitors (vorinostat, romidepsin) and EZH2 methyltransferase inhibitors (tazemetostat) are approved anticancer drugs targeting the nucleosome regulatory machinery. Histone H3 mutations (H3K27M) are oncogenic drivers in pediatric gliomas.

panels.caption: Side view of the nucleosome core particle showing 147 bp of DNA (orange/gray) wrapped 1.65 turns around the histone octamer. H3 (blue), H4 (green), H2A (yellow), H2B (red) are in distinct colors.
Top-down view showing the electropositive histone surface (blue) complementary to the electronegative DNA (red). The dyad axis of pseudo-symmetry is at the center.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Nucleosome core particle (1AOI) at 2.8 Å—the disc-shaped complex is ~11 nm in diameter; nucleosomes stack in chromatin to achieve 100,000-fold DNA compaction.

panels.caption: DNA-histone interface at one of the 14 contact points—an arginine residue (blue) inserts into the compressed minor groove (orange) at a DNA bending point. Repeated with pseudo-two-fold symmetry around the nucleosome.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: DNA-histone contact at the nucleosome core—arginine intercalation at minor groove positions bends DNA around the histone spool. Repeated 14 times per nucleosome.

key_facts: Nucleosome core particle solved at 2.8 Å by Luger, Mader, Richmond, Sargent, and Richmond at ETH Zurich, published in Nature in 1997.
147 bp of DNA wraps 1.65 turns around an octamer of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 histones (two copies each).
Fourteen DNA-histone contact points per half-nucleosome use arginine insertion into the minor groove to bend DNA.
Histone N-terminal tails are sites of acetylation, methylation, and phosphorylation—the epigenetic histone code.
The nucleosome provides ~10,000-fold DNA compaction; further looping achieves the full 100,000-fold compaction.
HDAC inhibitors (vorinostat) and EZH2 inhibitors (tazemetostat) target nucleosome regulatory enzymes and are approved anticancer drugs.
Histone H3 K27M mutation is an oncogenic driver in pediatric gliomas, directly disrupting epigenetic regulation.
significance: The nucleosome structure explained chromatin compaction and provided the molecular foundation for epigenetics. Every aspect of gene regulation in eukaryotes involves nucleosome positioning, remodeling, and histone modification. The structure enabled development of epigenetic drugs approved for lymphoma, myeloma, and pediatric brain tumors.

name: GroEL-GroES Chaperonin
title: The Anfinsen Cage: GroEL-GroES and the Molecular Mechanism of Protein Folding
abstract: The GroEL-GroES chaperonin complex is a molecular machine that encapsulates misfolded proteins and provides a protected environment for refolding. Zhaohui Xu, Ana Horwich, and Paul Sigler solved the 3.0 Å crystal structure in 1997 at Yale, revealing the dramatic conformational changes that couple ATP hydrolysis to substrate refolding inside the Anfinsen cage.

sections.content: A Cage for Protein Folding

In 1997, Zhaohui Xu, Ana L. Horwich, and Paul B. Sigler at Yale University published the 3.0 Å crystal structure of the GroEL-GroES complex in Nature. GroEL is a double-ring complex of 14 identical 57 kDa subunits (7 per ring); GroES is a single ring of 7 identical 10 kDa subunits that caps one GroEL ring, sealing the folding chamber.
See Fig. 1
Conformational Cycle and the Anfinsen Cage

In the GroES-bound state, the GroEL apical domains rotate ~60 degrees and elevate ~25 Å, transforming the hydrophobic substrate-binding surface into a hydrophilic inner surface—the Anfinsen cage. This 175,000 cubic angstrom chamber isolates a single substrate protein from the crowded cytoplasm, allowing it to fold without aggregation. ATP hydrolysis in the cis ring ejects GroES and releases the substrate after ~10 seconds.
See Fig. 2
Disease Relevance and Therapeutic Targeting

Human Hsp60 (GroEL homolog) is essential for mitochondrial protein folding; Hsp60 mutations cause hereditary spastic paraplegia. The eukaryotic GroEL homolog TRiC/CCT is required for folding actin, tubulin, and huntingtin—relevant to Huntington's disease. Inhibitors of bacterial chaperonins are under investigation as antibiotics.

panels.caption: Side view of the GroEL-GroES complex showing the two GroEL rings (14 subunits, alternating blue/cyan) and the GroES cap (yellow). The cis folding chamber is enclosed between the GroES cap and the upper GroEL ring.
Cross-sectional view of GroEL-GroES revealing the enclosed cis folding chamber. The inner surface of the GroES-bound ring is hydrophilic (blue), preventing substrate aggregation.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: GroEL-GroES chaperonin (1AON) at 3.0 Å—the 840 kDa complex forms an ATP-driven molecular chamber that folds denatured proteins in isolation.

panels.caption: GroEL-GroES interface showing GroES mobile loops (yellow sticks) inserting into pockets on the GroEL apical domain (blue). This interaction triggers the 60-degree apical domain rotation that seals the folding chamber.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: GroEL-GroES binding interface—the GroES mobile loop contacts trigger the apical domain rotation that seals the folding chamber.

key_facts: GroEL-GroES solved at 3.0 Å by Xu, Horwich, and Sigler at Yale, published in Nature in 1997.
GroEL is a 14-mer double ring (7+7 subunits, each 57 kDa); GroES is a 7-mer cap (10 kDa per subunit).
The Anfinsen cage: the enclosed folding chamber prevents aggregation by isolating substrate from the crowded cytoplasm.
ATP hydrolysis drives an ~60-degree apical domain rotation converting the hydrophobic inner surface to hydrophilic, releasing substrate.
Human Hsp60 (GroEL homolog) is essential for mitochondrial protein folding; Hsp60 mutations cause hereditary spastic paraplegia.
TRiC/CCT, the eukaryotic GroEL homolog, is required for folding actin, tubulin, and mutant huntingtin.
GroEL assists folding of ~300 essential E. coli proteins including many beta-barrel and TIM barrel fold proteins.
significance: GroEL-GroES revealed that protein folding in the cell is an actively chaperonin-facilitated event, not merely spontaneous thermodynamic process. The Anfinsen cage concept resolved the paradox of how cells fold proteins reliably despite high concentration and aggregation propensity. This insight drives drug discovery targeting chaperone systems in cancer, neurodegeneration, and infectious disease.

name: 26S Proteasome
title: The Cell's Shredder: The 26S Proteasome and Targeted Protein Destruction
abstract: The 26S proteasome is the major protein degradation machine of eukaryotic cells, a 2.5 MDa complex that unfolds and cleaves polyubiquitinated proteins into short peptides. Andreas Schweitzer, Antje Aufderheide, and Wolfgang Baumeister determined the human 26S proteasome structure at 3.5 Å by cryo-EM in 2016. Bortezomib, which inhibits the proteasome's catalytic beta subunits, was the first proteasome inhibitor approved for cancer treatment.

sections.content: The Cellular Destruction Machine

In 2016, Andreas Schweitzer, Antje Aufderheide, Timm Rudack, Florian Beck, Gunter Pfeifer, Jurgen Plitzko, Eri Sakata, Klaus Schulten, Friedrich Forster, and Wolfgang Baumeister determined the human 26S proteasome at 3.5 Å by single-particle cryo-EM, published in PNAS. The complex consists of the 20S catalytic particle (a barrel-shaped four-ring stack of alpha and beta subunits) capped by one or two 19S regulatory particles that recognize ubiquitinated substrates and unfold them for threading into the catalytic chamber.
See Fig. 1
Catalytic Mechanism and Drug Targeting

The 20S core contains three types of proteolytic activity: chymotrypsin-like (beta5), trypsin-like (beta2), and caspase-like (beta1), provided by N-terminal threonine residues. Bortezomib (Velcade), a dipeptide boronic acid, reversibly inhibits the beta5 subunit by forming a covalent adduct with Thr1. Multiple myeloma cells, which produce massive quantities of immunoglobulin stressing the ubiquitin-proteasome system, are exquisitely sensitive to proteasome inhibition.
See Fig. 2
From Cancer Therapy to Basic Biology

Bortezomib (2003), carfilzomib (2012), and ixazomib (2015) are approved proteasome inhibitors for multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma. Parkinson's disease is associated with accumulation of ubiquitinated alpha-synuclein aggregates that overwhelm proteasomal capacity. The proteasome also generates 8-10 residue peptides for MHC class I antigen presentation.

panels.caption: Overall architecture of the human 26S proteasome showing the 20S catalytic particle (central barrel) flanked by the 19S regulatory particle. The 19S base contains six AAA-ATPase subunits that unfold and translocate substrates.
Cross-section of the 26S proteasome revealing the substrate entry pore of the 19S base aligned with the translocation channel through the 20S barrel.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Human 26S proteasome (5GJR) at 3.5 Å by cryo-EM—the 2.5 MDa complex processes polyubiquitinated substrates by unfolding through the 19S ATPase ring and cleaving in the 20S catalytic chamber.

panels.caption: 20S catalytic chamber showing the three active beta subunits: beta5 (chymotrypsin-like, blue), beta2 (trypsin-like, green), beta1 (caspase-like, red). N-terminal threonine nucleophiles are shown as sticks. Bortezomib binding site on beta5 is highlighted.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: 20S proteasome catalytic sites—three distinct proteolytic activities use N-terminal threonine residues as nucleophiles; bortezomib inhibits beta5 via covalent threonine adduct.

key_facts: Human 26S proteasome cryo-EM structure at 3.5 Å was determined by Schweitzer, Aufderheide, Rudack, Baumeister et al., published in PNAS in 2016.
The 2.5 MDa complex: 20S catalytic barrel (28 subunits) capped by the 19S regulatory particle (19 subunits) that recognizes ubiquitin tags.
Three catalytic activities (chymotrypsin-, trypsin-, caspase-like) reside in beta5, beta2, and beta1 subunits using N-terminal threonine nucleophiles.
Bortezomib (Velcade, 2003) inhibits beta5 via a reversible covalent boronic acid-threonine adduct—first approved proteasome inhibitor.
Multiple myeloma cells are especially sensitive to proteasome inhibition due to high immunoglobulin production causing proteotoxic stress.
The proteasome generates 8-10 residue peptides for MHC class I antigen presentation, linking it to adaptive immunity.
Parkinson's disease is associated with ubiquitinated alpha-synuclein aggregates that overwhelm proteasomal capacity.
significance: The high-resolution 26S proteasome structure revealed the complete molecular mechanism of the cell's primary protein degradation pathway. Bortezomib's success in multiple myeloma established the proteasome as a major drug target, and the structure now guides development of subunit-selective inhibitors and PROTAC degrader molecules that hijack the ubiquitin-proteasome system for targeted protein elimination.

name: RNA Polymerase II
title: Transcription at Atomic Resolution: RNA Polymerase II and the Nobel of Gene Readout
abstract: RNA polymerase II transcribes all protein-coding genes in eukaryotes. Patrick Cramer, David Bushnell, and Roger Kornberg solved the 2.8 Å crystal structure of yeast RNA pol II in 2001 at Stanford, revealing how the 12-subunit, 500 kDa enzyme clamps DNA and synthesizes RNA with extraordinary fidelity. This work earned Roger Kornberg the 2006 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

sections.content: Reading the Genome at Atomic Resolution

In 2001, Patrick Cramer, David A. Bushnell, and Roger D. Kornberg at Stanford University solved the 2.8 Å crystal structure of the complete 10-subunit yeast RNA polymerase II and published it in Science. The enzyme is a 514 kDa complex that transcribes all protein-coding genes in eukaryotes, moving along DNA at ~30 nucleotides per second with an error rate of ~1 per 100,000 incorporated nucleotides.
See Fig. 1
The Clamp, the Cleft, and the Bridge Helix

The Cramer structure revealed key architectural features: the mobile clamp domain that grips the DNA-RNA hybrid duplex; the central cleft between Rpb1 and Rpb2 accommodating the 9-bp hybrid; the bridge helix that assists translocation; and the trigger loop that folds upon NTP binding to catalyze phosphodiester bond formation. The active site Mg2+ ion is coordinated by Asp481 and Asp483 of Rpb1.
See Fig. 2
Nobel Prize and Medical Implications

Roger Kornberg received the 2006 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for molecular studies of eukaryotic transcription. Alpha-amanitin, the deadly toxin from Amanita phalloides mushrooms, inhibits RNA pol II by trapping the trigger loop—the structural basis of this inhibition is precisely known. CDK8 (part of the Mediator kinase module) is an emerging cancer drug target.

panels.caption: Overall architecture of yeast RNA pol II showing 10 subunits (Rpb1-Rpb10) in distinct colors. The mobile clamp domain (dark blue) grips the DNA-RNA hybrid.

Electrostatic surface of RNA pol II showing the positively charged central cleft (blue) that accommodates the negatively charged DNA-RNA hybrid. Upstream DNA entry and downstream exit channels are visible.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Yeast RNA polymerase II (1I6H) at 2.8 Å—the 500 kDa, 10-subunit enzyme orchestrates all mRNA synthesis in eukaryotes.

panels.caption: Active site of RNA pol II showing the catalytic Mg2+ ion (green sphere) coordinated by Asp481 and Asp483 of Rpb1. The bridge helix (orange) flanks the site where NTP is incorporated.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: RNA pol II active site—two-metal-ion catalytic mechanism uses Mg2+ to activate the 3'-OH nucleophile and stabilize the pyrophosphate leaving group.

key_facts: Yeast RNA pol II solved at 2.8 Å by Cramer, Bushnell, and Kornberg at Stanford, published in Science in 2001.
The 10-subunit, 514 kDa enzyme synthesizes all mRNA from protein-coding genes in eukaryotes at ~30 nucleotides per second.
The mobile clamp domain grips the 9-bp DNA-RNA hybrid; bridge helix and trigger loop coordinate translocation and catalysis.
Active site Mg2+ (coordinated by Asp481/Asp483 of Rpb1) activates the 3'-OH nucleophile via a two-metal-ion mechanism.
Roger Kornberg received the 2006 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for molecular studies of eukaryotic transcription.
Alpha-amanitin (Amanita mushroom toxin) inhibits RNA pol II by trapping the trigger loop, causing lethal liver failure.
CDK8 (Mediator kinase module) and BRD4 (pause-release) are emerging anticancer targets identified through RNA pol II structural biology.
significance: The RNA pol II structure completed the molecular picture of eukaryotic gene expression and provided the structural basis for understanding how all transcription factors, coactivators, and inhibitors regulate mRNA synthesis. Every human disease involving aberrant gene expression converges on RNA pol II. The structure directly guides development of transcription-targeting drugs for cancer and antiviral therapy.

name: IgG1 Antibody
title: The First Full-Length Antibody: IgG1 and the Architecture of Immune Defense
abstract: Immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) is the most abundant antibody class in human serum. Lester Harris, Stephen Larson, and Alexander McPherson determined the first complete crystal structure of a full-length murine IgG1 antibody at 2.7 Å in 1997, revealing the entire four-domain Y-shaped architecture. This landmark enabled rational design of therapeutic antibodies that became the dominant modality in modern biopharmaceuticals.

sections.content: The Complete Antibody Revealed

In 1997, Lester J. Harris, Stephen B. Larson, Kurt W. Hasel, and Alexander McPherson at the University of California, Riverside, solved the first full-length IgG1 antibody crystal structure at 2.7 Å and published it in Biochemistry. Previous work had solved Fab fragments and Fc regions separately; Harris and colleagues captured the intact Y-shaped molecule with both antigen-binding Fab arms, the Fc region, and the hinge in a single crystal lattice.
See Fig. 1
The Y-Shape and Functional Modularity

IgG1 consists of two heavy chains (gamma) and two light chains (kappa or lambda). Each Fab arm contains variable domains (VH and VL) that form the antigen-binding site (CDR loops), and constant domains (CH1 and CL). The Fc region contains CH2 and CH3 domains and mediates effector functions through Fcgamma receptors and complement. The flexible Pro-rich hinge allows independent motion of the two Fab arms.
See Fig. 2
Therapeutic Antibodies and Fc Engineering

The full-length antibody structure enabled rational engineering of therapeutic antibodies: CDR grafting (humanization), Fc engineering to extend half-life (YTE mutation), enhance ADCC (GASDALIE), or abolish effector function (LALA-PG). Over 100 therapeutic antibodies are now approved. Adalimumab (Humira) was the best-selling drug in the world for a decade with over $20 billion in annual sales.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of full-length murine IgG1 showing the Y-shape. Two heavy chains (blue, red) and two light chains (green, yellow) form the complete antibody. The two Fab arms project upward; the Fc region is at the base.
Molecular surface of IgG1 showing the electropositive CDR region at the top of each Fab arm and the Fc region below the hinge.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Full-length murine IgG1 antibody (1IGT) at 2.7 Å—the first complete antibody structure showing functional modularity: antigen recognition (Fab) is separated from effector function (Fc) by the flexible hinge.

panels.caption: CDR loops of the IgG1 Fab arm showing the six hypervariable loops (CDR-H1, H2, H3, CDR-L1, L2, L3) forming the antigen-binding paratope. CDR-H3 (orange, longest and most variable) contacts the center of the antigen epitope.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: CDR loops of IgG1—the six CDR loops encoded by recombined V, D, and J gene segments create the immense antibody diversity of the adaptive immune system.

key_facts: First full-length IgG1 crystal structure solved at 2.7 Å by Harris, Larson, Hasel, and McPherson at UC Riverside, published in Biochemistry in 1997.
IgG1 is a heterotetrameric Y-shaped molecule: two heavy chains (~50 kDa) + two light chains (~25 kDa), linked by disulfide bonds.
Six CDR loops (3 per Fab arm, from VH and VL) determine antigen specificity; CDR-H3 is the most variable and dominant contact loop.
Fc region CH2/CH3 domains mediate effector functions through FcgammaR receptors (ADCC, phagocytosis) and FcRn (half-life extension).
Over 100 therapeutic antibodies are approved, making IgG the dominant biopharmaceutical modality by revenue.
Adalimumab (anti-TNF IgG1) was the best-selling drug globally for a decade with >$20B annual peak revenue.
Fc engineering mutations (YTE: M252Y/S254T/T256E) extend antibody half-life 3-4 fold by enhancing FcRn binding at acidic endosomal pH.
significance: The first full-length IgG structure provided the complete structural blueprint for the antibody scaffold underlying the modern biopharmaceutical industry. By revealing how Fab and Fc regions connect and move, the structure enabled rational engineering of half-life, effector function, and bispecificity. Therapeutic antibodies now account for over 40% of global pharmaceutical revenue.

name: SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein
title: The Pandemic Antigen: SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein and mRNA Vaccine Design
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein mediates viral entry by binding the ACE2 receptor and fusing viral and host membranes. Alexandra Walls, Young-Jun Park, and David Veesler solved the cryo-EM structure of the prefusion spike trimer at 3.2 Å in 2020, weeks after the virus was sequenced. The structure directly guided design of mRNA vaccines achieving extraordinary efficacy in the COVID-19 pandemic.

sections.content: A Structure in Record Time

In February 2020, Alexandra Walls, Young-Jun Park, M. Alexandra Tortorici, Abigail Wall, Andrew T. McGuire, and David Veesler at the University of Washington published the 3.2 Å cryo-EM structure of the full-length SARS-CoV-2 spike in Cell. A parallel structure was published simultaneously by Jason McLellan's group at UT Austin. The speed of this work was enabled by prior investment in coronavirus structural biology and cryo-EM infrastructure.
See Fig. 1
Prefusion Trimer and ACE2 Recognition

The spike is a homotrimer (~4.5 MDa); each protomer contains NTD, receptor-binding domain (RBD), and two S2 subunit heptad repeats that drive membrane fusion. The RBD opens ('up' conformation) to engage ACE2 and closes ('down') to evade immune recognition. The furin cleavage site (RRAR) between S1 and S2 is critical for SARS-CoV-2 transmissibility. Six proline substitutions (2P or 6P) introduced into S2 lock the trimer in prefusion conformation, enhancing neutralizing antibody responses.
See Fig. 2
mRNA Vaccines and Variant Evolution

The BNT162b2 (Pfizer/BioNTech) and mRNA-1273 (Moderna) vaccines encode the 2P proline-stabilized spike directly implementing the structural design principle. These vaccines achieved ~95% efficacy—the highest of any respiratory virus vaccine. Structural surveillance of variants (Alpha through Omicron) revealed how RBD mutations alter ACE2 affinity and antibody evasion, informing bivalent vaccine formulations in real time.

panels.caption: Cryo-EM structure of SARS-CoV-2 spike trimer in prefusion conformation. Three protomers (blue, red, green) are shown. One RBD is in the 'up' (open) conformation exposed for ACE2 binding.
Electrostatic surface of the spike trimer showing the electropositive ACE2 binding ridge on the RBD (one protomer in 'up' conformation) and the heavily glycosylated outer surface.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (6VYB) at 3.2 Å by cryo-EM—the trimeric prefusion conformation encoded by all mRNA COVID-19 vaccines.

panels.caption: RBD in 'up' conformation showing the receptor-binding motif (RBM, orange) that contacts ACE2. Key residues mutated in variants of concern (K417, L452, E484, N501) are shown as sticks. The furin cleavage site (RRAR, yellow) connecting S1 and S2 is indicated.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: SARS-CoV-2 RBD receptor-binding motif—Omicron mutations cluster in this region, simultaneously enhancing ACE2 affinity and evading neutralizing antibodies.

key_facts: SARS-CoV-2 spike prefusion cryo-EM structure (3.2 Å) solved by Walls, Park, Tortorici, Veesler et al. at U. Washington, published in Cell in February 2020.
The homotrimeric spike (~4.5 MDa with glycans) uses the RBD to engage ACE2; one to three RBDs can be in 'up' conformation per trimer.
Six proline substitutions (2P or 6P) in S2 lock the spike in prefusion conformation, dramatically enhancing vaccine-induced neutralizing antibody responses.
BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 mRNA vaccines encode the 2P-stabilized spike; both achieved ~95% efficacy against the original SARS-CoV-2 strain.
Omicron variant carries >30 mutations in the spike, including 15 in the RBD, driving both immune evasion and enhanced ACE2 binding.
The furin cleavage site (RRAR insert) between S1 and S2, absent in SARS-CoV-1, is a key determinant of SARS-CoV-2 high transmissibility.
The 2P prefusion-stabilization strategy is now standard for RSV, influenza, and HIV vaccine design.
significance: The SARS-CoV-2 spike structure, solved within weeks of the pandemic's emergence, directly enabled vaccine design that ended the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic. The proline-stabilized prefusion antigen strategy produced vaccines with >95% efficacy in under a year—the fastest vaccine development in history. The structure provides a real-time example of how structural biology accelerates public health response to infectious disease.

name: Beta-2AR-Gs Complex
title: Signal Transmission Captured: The First GPCR-G Protein Complex Structure
abstract: The complex between the beta-2 adrenergic receptor and the heterotrimeric Gs protein was the first structure to capture a GPCR in its active, G protein-coupled state. Soren Rasmussen, Brian DeVree, and Brian Kobilka's group solved the 3.2 Å crystal structure in 2011, revealing the dramatic conformational changes in the receptor that open the cytoplasmic G protein-binding cavity.

sections.content: Catching the Signal Mid-Flight

In 2011, Soren G. F. Rasmussen, Brian T. DeVree, Yaozhong Zou, Andrew C. Kruse, Ka Young Chung, Tong Sun Kobilka, Brian K. Kobilka, and Roger K. Sunahara published the 3.2 Å structure of the beta2AR-Gs complex in Nature, completing the mechanistic picture of GPCR signal transduction started by the 2007 beta2AR structure.
See Fig. 1
The Open Cytoplasmic Cavity

Comparison of active beta2AR-Gs with the inactive beta2AR structure (2007) revealed that agonist binding drives a 14 Å outward movement of transmembrane helix 6 (TM6), opening a large cavity that accommodates the Galpha-s alpha5 helix. The alpha5 helix inserts 8 Å into the receptor core and directly connects to the nucleotide-binding pocket of Galpha-s, explaining how agonist binding >30 Å away stimulates GDP release and G protein activation.
See Fig. 2
Impact on Drug Discovery

The beta2AR-Gs structure revealed the basis for G protein selectivity and provided a framework for designing biased agonists that selectively activate G protein signaling without activating beta-arrestin recruitment. Biased agonists at mu-opioid receptors (Gi-biased) were developed as potential analgesics with reduced respiratory depression; biased agonists at GLP-1R are being pursued for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

panels.caption: Complete beta2AR-Gs complex. The beta2AR (blue, seven transmembrane helices) is bound to agonist BI-167107 (yellow sticks) at the extracellular face and to the Galpha-s subunit (orange) at the intracellular face. Gbeta (green) and Ggamma (red) complete the heterotrimer.
Side view showing the membrane plane. TM6 is displaced outward by 14 Å relative to the inactive receptor, creating the cytoplasmic cavity that accommodates the Galpha-s alpha5 helix.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: beta2AR-Gs complex (3SN6) at 3.2 Å—the first GPCR-G protein complex, capturing signal transduction in atomic detail from agonist-binding site to G protein nucleotide pocket.

panels.caption: beta2AR-Galpha-s interface showing the Galpha-s alpha5 helix (orange) inserted 8 Å into the TM6 outward-displaced cavity. Key contacts between Galpha-s Leu393, Ile394 and receptor Arg131, Tyr326 are shown.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: beta2AR-Galpha-s coupling interface—the alpha5 helix mechanically transmits the TM6 movement to open the GDP-binding site and trigger nucleotide exchange.

key_facts: beta2AR-Gs complex solved at 3.2 Å by Rasmussen, DeVree, Kobilka, Sunahara et al., published in Nature in 2011.
TM6 moves outward by 14 Å upon receptor activation—the largest conformational change observed in a GPCR activation.
The Galpha-s alpha5 helix inserts 8 Å into the cytoplasmic cavity and directly connects to the GDP-binding site, triggering nucleotide exchange.
A T4 lysozyme and nanobody were required to stabilize the transient complex.
Biased agonism concept emerged from comparing active and inactive GPCR structures.
The structure provides the framework for designing selective modulators of Gs, Gi, and Gq coupling for heart failure, pain, and metabolic disease.
Kobilka's 2007 (inactive) and 2011 (active beta2AR-Gs) structures together provided the complete mechanistic picture honored by the 2012 Nobel Prize.
significance: The beta2AR-Gs complex structure completed the mechanistic picture of G protein-coupled signaling, revealing how extracellular ligand binding is transmitted across the membrane to activate an intracellular G protein. This enabled structure-based design of biased agonists selectively engaging beneficial G protein signaling—a strategy now applied to opioids, glucagon receptors, and dozens of other GPCRs.

name: Collagen Triple Helix
title: The Body's Scaffold: Collagen and the Most Abundant Protein in the Human Body
abstract: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, comprising one-third of total protein mass and providing tensile strength to skin, bone, tendon, and blood vessels. Jordi Bella, Manu Eaton, Barbara Brodsky, and Helen Berman solved the 1.9 Å crystal structure of a synthetic collagen triple-helical peptide in 1994, explaining how hydroxyproline stabilizes the helix and how collagen mutations cause brittle bone disease.

sections.content: The Rope That Holds the Body Together

In 1994, Jordi Bella, Manu Eaton, Barbara Brodsky, and Helen M. Berman at Rutgers University solved the 1.9 Å crystal structure of the collagen model peptide (Pro-Hyp-Gly)10 and published it in Science. Collagen's triple helix—three chains wound around each other in a right-handed superhelix—had been known from fiber diffraction since the 1950s (Ramachandran and Kartha, 1954), but the Bella structure provided the first atomic-resolution picture of hydrogen bonding, water structure, and hydroxyproline contacts.
See Fig. 1
Hydroxyproline and Thermal Stability

The Bella structure revealed that hydroxyproline (Hyp) residues mediate water-bridged hydrogen bonds to backbone carbonyls of neighboring chains. The 4R-hydroxy group electronegatively destabilizes the ring pucker conformation unfavorable in the triple helix, biasing the residue toward the correct polyproline II conformation. This explains why vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy: unhydroxylated proline cannot stabilize the triple helix.
See Fig. 2
Disease: Osteogenesis Imperfecta and Beyond

Over 1,400 mutations in COL1A1 and COL1A2 cause osteogenesis imperfecta ('brittle bone disease'). Structurally, Gly substitutions introduce bulges that nucleate unfolding—the Gly-Xaa-Yaa triplet requires glycine at every third position. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Alport syndrome also arise from collagen mutations. Collagen is the scaffold for tissue engineering, wound healing matrices, and injectable soft-tissue fillers.

panels.caption: Collagen triple helix (1CGD) showing three polyproline II-type chains (cyan, magenta, yellow) wound in a right-handed superhelix. The characteristic 1/3 stagger between chains is visible. Hydroxyproline residues are shown as sticks.
Stick representation showing the backbone hydrogen bond network. Each NH of glycine (blue) hydrogen-bonds to the CO of the Xaa position on the preceding chain.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Collagen triple helix (1CGD) at 1.9 Å—three chains offset by one residue, wound into a right-handed superhelix with a pitch of 86 Å and 10 triplets per turn.

panels.caption: Hydroxyproline residues in the collagen triple helix with water molecules (red spheres) bridging the Hyp hydroxyl groups to backbone carbonyls of neighboring chains—the primary source of helix stabilization.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: Hydroxyproline-water network in collagen—the 4R-Hyp hydroxyl coordinates water molecules hydrogen-bonding across chains, explaining why vitamin C deficiency causes structural failure in scurvy.

key_facts: Collagen triple helix solved at 1.9 Å by Bella, Eaton, Brodsky, and Berman at Rutgers, published in Science in 1994.
Collagen is the most abundant protein in humans (~30% of total protein), providing tensile strength to skin, bone, tendon, and blood vessels.
The (Gly-Xaa-Yaa)n sequence requires glycine (the smallest amino acid) at every third position to fit the tight triple helix core.
Hydroxyproline (requires vitamin C for biosynthesis) stabilizes the triple helix via water-mediated hydrogen bonds—structural basis of scurvy.
Over 1,400 mutations in COL1A1/COL1A2 cause osteogenesis imperfecta; Gly substitutions introduce steric clashes nucleating triple helix unfolding.
28 collagen types exist in humans (Types I-XXVIII), each with distinct tissue distribution and mechanical properties.
Collagen is the scaffold for tissue engineering, wound healing matrices, and soft-tissue fillers in cosmetic medicine.
significance: The atomic-resolution collagen structure explained the molecular basis of the most abundant structural protein in the body, resolving questions about hydroxyproline's role in helix stability and the mechanism of osteogenesis imperfecta mutations. This knowledge underpins rational approaches to collagen-related diseases, guides engineering of collagen biomaterials for tissue repair, and explains why vitamin C is essential for structural integrity.

name: F-Actin
title: The Cytoskeleton at Near-Atomic Resolution: F-Actin and Cell Movement
abstract: Filamentous actin (F-actin) is the polymeric form of actin that forms the core of the cytoskeleton, driving cell movement, division, and shape. Hsiau-Wei Chou and Daved Bhatt solved the cryo-EM structure of rabbit skeletal F-actin at 3.1 Å in 2018 at the MRC-LMB, providing the highest-resolution F-actin structure to that point and revealing the conformational changes between monomeric G-actin and filamentous F-actin in atomic detail.

sections.content: The Filament That Moves Cells

In 2018, Hsiau-Wei Chou and Daved Bhatt at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology published the 3.1 Å cryo-EM structure of rabbit skeletal F-actin in PNAS. Actin polymerizes from G-actin (globular) monomers into F-actin (filamentous) helical polymers. F-actin is a left-handed double helix with a 36 nm crossover repeat, providing the tracks for myosin motors and the scaffolding for branched networks driven by the Arp2/3 complex.
See Fig. 1
G-Actin to F-Actin: The Structural Transition

Comparison of G-actin and F-actin reveals a ~20-degree flattening of the actin monomer upon polymerization, driven by contacts between the D-loop of one monomer and the hydrophobic plug of the next. The D-loop becomes ordered in the filament—disordered in G-actin—forming the key longitudinal contact. ADP in F-actin adopts a more closed nucleotide-pocket conformation than ATP-bound G-actin, controlling filament dynamics.
See Fig. 2
Drug Targets and Pathogen Exploitation

Phalloidin (Amanita toxin) stabilizes F-actin by binding between subunits; latrunculin sequesters G-actin monomers. These compounds are used in cell biology research and as lead structures for anticancer drugs targeting cytoskeletal dynamics in cancer metastasis. Bacterial pathogens (Listeria, Shigella) hijack actin polymerization for intracellular motility—the F-actin structure explains how bacterial surface proteins nucleate actin assembly.

panels.caption: Cryo-EM structure of F-actin filament segment showing seven actin subunits (alternating blue/cyan) in the left-handed helical arrangement. ADP (yellow sticks) is visible in each subunit's nucleotide cleft.

Surface of F-actin filament colored by hydrophobicity. The inter-subunit contacts include a prominent hydrophobic plug (orange) that inserts between the D-loop and subdomain 3 of the adjacent subunit.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: F-actin (6OGE) at 3.1 Å by cryo-EM—left-handed double-stranded helix with 36 nm crossover repeat, 166-degree rotation and 27.5 Å axial rise per subunit.

panels.caption: Inter-subunit interface of F-actin showing the D-loop (blue, ordered only in the filament) contacting the hydrophobic plug region (orange) of the adjacent subunit. Residues Ile287, Met269, Phe262, and Val43 form a hydrophobic cluster.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: F-actin longitudinal interface—the D-loop becomes ordered upon polymerization and inserts into the hydrophobic cleft of the next subunit, stabilizing the filament and explaining cooperativity of actin polymerization.

key_facts: F-actin cryo-EM structure at 3.1 Å determined by Chou and Bhatt at the MRC-LMB, published in PNAS in 2018.
F-actin is a left-handed double helix with 36 nm crossover repeat, 166-degree rotation, and 27.5 Å rise per subunit.
The G-actin to F-actin transition involves a ~20-degree monomer flattening and ordering of the D-loop that inserts into the adjacent subunit.
F-actin is the track for myosin II (muscle contraction), myosin V (vesicle transport), and scaffold for Arp2/3-branched lamellipodia.
Phalloidin (Amanita toxin) binds between actin subunits to stabilize filaments and is used ubiquitously as a fluorescent F-actin probe.
Actin cytoskeleton remodeling drives cancer invasion and metastasis; anti-actin compounds are in development as anti-metastatic drugs.
Bacterial pathogens (Listeria, Shigella) polymerize host actin via surface proteins (ActA, IcsA) for intracellular propulsion.
significance: The near-atomic F-actin structure resolved the conformational differences between monomeric and filamentous actin governing cytoskeleton dynamics—the engine of cell movement, division, and shape change. This knowledge underpins understanding of cancer metastasis, muscle contraction diseases, and the molecular strategies used by intracellular pathogens. F-actin structural biology now guides development of anti-metastatic compounds.

name: Streptavidin-Biotin
title: The Strongest Non-Covalent Bond: Streptavidin-Biotin as a Universal Biotechnology Tool
abstract: The streptavidin-biotin complex exhibits the strongest known non-covalent interaction in biology, with a dissociation constant of approximately 10^-14 M. Patrick Weber, David Ohlendorf, John Wendoloski, and Fred Salemme solved the 2.6 Å crystal structure of Streptomyces avidinii streptavidin in 1989, revealing the beta-barrel scaffold and deep hydrophobic biotin-binding pocket responsible for the extraordinary affinity.

sections.content: A Bond Near the Limit of Non-Covalency

In 1989, Patrick C. Weber, David H. Ohlendorf, John J. Wendoloski, and Fred R. Salemme at Bristol-Myers Squibb published the 2.6 Å crystal structure of Streptomyces avidinii streptavidin in Science. The dissociation constant for biotin (Kd ~10^-14 M) corresponds to a binding free energy of ~19 kcal/mol—approximately 6-fold stronger than a typical enzyme-substrate interaction and only 2-fold weaker than a covalent bond at physiological temperature.
See Fig. 1
The Barrel and the Buried Pocket

Streptavidin is a homotetramer; each subunit adopts an eight-stranded beta-barrel (jellyroll fold) with the biotin-binding pocket buried at one end. Biotin is buried to 84% of its surface area, forming hydrogen bonds with Asn23, Ser27, Tyr43, Asn49, and Ser45 and a stacking interaction with Trp92 that contributes ~3 kcal/mol. The extraordinary affinity arises from nearly complete desolvation of the ligand combined with a tight hydrogen bond network.
See Fig. 2
Biotechnology Platform

The streptavidin-biotin interaction survives denaturing agents, extremes of pH, temperature, and organic solvents, making it the universal coupling agent in biotechnology: ELISA, Western blotting, flow cytometry, single-molecule force spectroscopy, biosensors, and targeted drug delivery. Engineered monomeric streptavidin (mSA) has been developed to avoid multivalent crosslinking artefacts in cell biology.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of streptavidin tetramer viewed from the biotin-binding face. Four subunits (distinct colors) each contribute an eight-stranded beta-barrel (jellyroll). Biotin molecules (yellow sticks) are visible buried at the end of each barrel.
Molecular surface of streptavidin showing four deep hydrophobic pockets (orange) that accommodate biotin. The non-polar nature of the binding site explains biotin's 84% burial and near-zero off-rate.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Streptavidin-biotin complex (2BNH) at 2.6 Å—the homotetramer binds four biotin molecules with Kd ~10^-14 M, the strongest non-covalent interaction in nature.

panels.caption: Streptavidin biotin-binding site showing biotin (yellow) hydrogen bonded to Asn23, Ser27, Tyr43, Ser45, Asn49, and Asp128 (pink sticks) and stacked against Trp92 (orange). Five hydrogen bonds and the tryptophan stack account for >15 kcal/mol of binding energy.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: Streptavidin biotin-binding pocket—five direct hydrogen bonds plus aromatic stacking with Trp92 and near-complete desolvation of biotin produce the strongest known non-covalent interaction in biology.

key_facts: Streptavidin solved at 2.6 Å by Weber, Ohlendorf, Wendoloski, and Salemme at Bristol-Myers Squibb, published in Science in 1989.
The streptavidin-biotin Kd (~10^-14 M) is the strongest known non-covalent interaction in biology, with a half-life >24 hours at 37 degrees C.
Each subunit of the homotetramer forms an 8-stranded beta-barrel with a deep, hydrophobic biotin-binding pocket.
Biotin is 84% buried upon binding, forming 5 direct hydrogen bonds and a critical Trp92 aromatic stack; survives SDS, extremes of pH, and >100 degrees C.
The streptavidin-biotin interaction underpins ELISA, Western blotting, biosensors, SPR, cell sorting, and targeted drug delivery.
Engineered monomeric streptavidin (mSA, Kd ~10^-9 M) is used where monovalency is required to avoid crosslinking artefacts.
Egg white avidin (Kd ~10^-15 M) is the equivalent in higher organisms; convergently evolved the same binding geometry as streptavidin.
significance: The streptavidin structure explained the extraordinary affinity for biotin at atomic resolution and validated the use of this interaction as the near-universal molecular coupling system in biotechnology. No other non-covalent interaction combines such extraordinary affinity with chemical robustness. The streptavidin-biotin system underpins thousands of diagnostic and research applications.

name: Cas12a (Cpf1)
title: The Staggered Cutter: Cas12a and the Expansion of the CRISPR Toolkit
abstract: Cas12a (formerly Cpf1) is a Class 2, Type V CRISPR-Cas effector nuclease that generates staggered DNA cuts and uses only a crRNA without tracrRNA, distinguishing it from Cas9. Kazuki Yamano and colleagues in Feng Zhang's group solved the 2.8 Å crystal structure of Acidaminococcus sp. Cas12a in 2016, revealing the RuvC-only nuclease architecture and pre-ordered seed region that make Cas12a valuable for genome editing at T-rich PAM sites and for nucleic acid diagnostics.

sections.content: A Different CRISPR Cutter

In 2016, Kazuki Yamano, Bernd Zetsche, Rhiannon N. Smargon, Omar O. Abudayyeh, David Scott, and Feng Zhang solved the 2.8 Å crystal structure of Acidaminococcus sp. Cas12a (AsCas12a) in the binary complex with its crRNA, published in Cell. Unlike Cas9, which requires a tracrRNA and generates blunt cuts, Cas12a uses a single ~42-nucleotide crRNA and generates staggered 5-nt 5' overhangs. Its PAM sequence (5'-TTTN-3') is T-rich, complementing Cas9's NGG PAM.
See Fig. 1
RuvC Nuclease and the Pre-Ordered Seed

The Yamano structure revealed that Cas12a has only a single RuvC nuclease domain (vs. Cas9's RuvC plus HNH), which cleaves both DNA strands sequentially. The seed region of the crRNA (positions 1-5 adjacent to the PAM) is pre-ordered in a helix in the binary complex, facilitating rapid target search. The structure also revealed the collateral cleavage activity of Cas12a (activated single-stranded DNA degradation) that underlies the DETECTR diagnostic platform.
See Fig. 2
Diagnostics and Therapeutic Applications

Cas12a's collateral ssDNA cleavage activity was harnessed in the DETECTR diagnostics platform, which can detect attomolar concentrations of specific DNA sequences in under an hour and was authorized for emergency use for COVID-19 detection. Cas12a's smaller size (1,228 aa vs. SpCas9's 1,368 aa) enables better AAV delivery for in vivo gene therapy.

Electrostatic surface of Cas12a showing the positively charged nucleic acid binding groove (blue) accommodating the crRNA:DNA heteroduplex. The PAM-interacting domain (bottom right) is electropositive to contact the T-rich PAM duplex.
