key_facts: AsCas12a-crRNA binary complex solved at 2.8 Å by Yamano, Zetsche, Smargon, Zhang et al., published in Cell in 2016.
Cas12a uses only a single ~42-nt crRNA (no tracrRNA), generates staggered 5-nt 5' overhangs, and requires a 5'-TTTN-3' PAM.
Single RuvC nuclease domain cleaves both DNA strands sequentially; no HNH domain (present in Cas9).
Pre-ordered seed region (positions 1-5 of spacer) facilitates rapid target search without conformational rearrangement.
Collateral ssDNA cleavage of Cas12a was harnessed in DETECTR diagnostics—attomolar DNA detection in under 1 hour, authorized for COVID-19 use.
Cas12a's smaller size (1,228 aa vs. SpCas9 1,368 aa) improves packaging into single AAV vectors for in vivo gene therapy.
Multiple Cas12a orthologs (LbCas12a, AsCas12a, FnCas12a) with distinct PAM preferences expand the addressable genome for editing.
significance: The Cas12a structure expanded the CRISPR toolkit beyond Cas9 with distinct properties: staggered cuts for improved HDR, T-rich PAM for AT-rich genome editing, and collateral ssDNA cleavage for ultrasensitive diagnostics. DETECTR, built directly on the structural understanding of Cas12a's catalytic mechanism, is now an FDA-authorized diagnostic platform.

name: Kinesin Motor Domain
title: The Cellular Walker: Kinesin and the Molecular Mechanism of Intracellular Transport
abstract: Kinesin-1 is a molecular motor that walks processively along microtubules, carrying cargo over micrometer distances at the cost of ATP hydrolysis. F. Jon Kull, Edward Sablin, Richard Lowe, Robert Fletterick, and Ronald Vale solved the 1.8 Å crystal structure of the rat kinesin motor domain in 1996 at UCSF, revealing unexpected structural homology to myosin and G proteins and establishing the framework for understanding chemomechanical coupling.

sections.content: The Motor That Walks on Protein Tracks

In 1996, F. Jon Kull, Edward P. Sablin, Richard Lowe, Robert J. Fletterick, and Ronald D. Vale at UCSF published the 1.8 Å crystal structure of the rat kinesin motor domain in Nature. Kinesin-1 moves processively toward microtubule plus ends, taking 8 nm steps (one tubulin dimer) per ATP hydrolysis cycle. Two motor domains operate in a hand-over-hand mechanism, powered by the conformational change in the neck linker upon ATP binding.
See Fig. 1
A Motor Fold Shared by Myosin and G Proteins

The Kull structure revealed that the kinesin motor domain is structurally homologous to both the myosin motor domain and the G protein alpha-subunit fold—all use a P-loop NTPase mechanism. The P-loop (Walker A, GQTSSGK), switch I, and switch II regions couple nucleotide state to the conformation of the neck linker, a ~12-residue peptide that docks onto the motor domain in the ATP state, generating the power stroke that propels cargo forward.
See Fig. 2
Disease and Drug Targeting

Mutations in KIF1B (kinesin-3) cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A; KIF5A mutations cause hereditary spastic paraplegia. In cancer, Eg5 (kinesin-5/KIF11) drives bipolar spindle formation and is an attractive mitotic target: ispinesib and SB-743921 entered clinical trials as Eg5 inhibitors. Cancer cells depend on kinesin-driven mitosis for their rapid proliferation.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of rat kinesin motor domain showing the central beta-sheet core (yellow) flanked by alpha-helices (red). The P-loop (GQTSSGK, blue) that binds nucleotide phosphates and switch I/II loops are indicated. ADP (yellow sticks) is visible in the nucleotide pocket.
Electrostatic surface of kinesin motor domain showing the microtubule-binding interface (positively charged, blue, bottom) and the nucleotide-binding site (mixed charge, center).

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Rat kinesin motor domain (3KIN) at 1.8 Å—the P-loop NTPase fold is structurally conserved with myosin and G proteins, revealing that cellular motors and signaling GTPases share a common evolutionary ancestor.

panels.caption: Nucleotide-binding site of kinesin showing ADP (yellow) coordinated by the P-loop (Walker A, blue sticks), switch I (Arg204, green), and switch II (Asp231-Leu234, red). The Mg2+ ion (green sphere) bridges the beta-phosphate of ADP and switch I.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: Kinesin P-loop NTPase active site—ATP hydrolysis rearranges switch I and II conformations, propagating to the neck linker to generate directed mechanical movement.

key_facts: Rat kinesin motor domain solved at 1.8 Å by Kull, Sablin, Lowe, Fletterick, and Vale at UCSF, published in Nature in 1996.
Kinesin takes 8 nm steps (one tubulin dimer length) per ATP hydrolysis cycle using a hand-over-hand mechanism.
The kinesin motor fold is homologous to myosin and G proteins—all use the P-loop NTPase (Walker A/B, switch I/II) mechanism.
ATP hydrolysis drives neck linker docking onto the motor domain, generating the ~60-degree rotation constituting the power stroke.
KIF1B mutations cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A; KIF5A mutations cause hereditary spastic paraplegia.
Eg5/KIF11 (kinesin-5) drives bipolar spindle assembly; Eg5 inhibitors (ispinesib, SB-743921) have entered Phase I/II cancer trials.
Neurons depend critically on kinesin for axonal transport of organelles, mRNAs, and neurofilaments over meter-long distances.
significance: The kinesin motor domain structure revealed that cells use a single evolutionary P-loop NTPase fold to power both molecular motors and GTPase signaling switches—connecting two fundamental cellular processes. The structure established the framework for understanding all 45 human kinesin family members, several essential for mitosis and targeted by anticancer inhibitors. Understanding kinesin-driven axonal transport is central to neurodegenerative disease biology.

name: Taq DNA Polymerase
title: The PCR Engine: Taq Polymerase and the Structure Behind the Biotechnology Revolution
abstract: Thermus aquaticus DNA polymerase I (Taq polymerase) is the thermostable enzyme that made PCR practical, earning Kary Mullis the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Yunliang Li, Sergey Korolev, and Gudrun Waksman solved the 2.3 Å crystal structure of the large Klenow-like fragment of Taq polymerase in 1998, revealing the 'right-hand' fold and the O-helix that closes over the dNTP to ensure fidelity during PCR extension.

sections.content: The Enzyme That Made PCR Possible

In 1998, Yunliang Li, Sergey Korolev, and Gudrun Waksman at Washington University in St. Louis published the 2.3 Å crystal structure of the Taq polymerase Klenow fragment in Structure. Kary Mullis conceived PCR in 1983 and earned the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus (Yellowstone hot springs, Chien et al. 1976) solved the need to add fresh enzyme after each 95-degree denaturation step, enabling automated thermocycling.
See Fig. 1
The Right-Hand Fold and O-Helix

The Taq polymerase structure revealed the classic DNA polymerase 'right-hand' fold: palm (catalytic core with conserved Asp residues), fingers (dNTP binding, O-helix), and thumb (duplex gripping) subdomains. The O-helix undergoes a ~40-degree rotation upon dNTP binding, closing over the nascent base pair to create the active site geometry that ensures Watson-Crick selectivity. Unlike Klenow fragment, Taq lacks a 3'-5' proofreading exonuclease domain, giving an error rate of ~1 per 10,000 nt.
See Fig. 2
Clinical and Diagnostic Impact

PCR enabled by Taq polymerase transformed clinical diagnostics: HIV viral load, HCV, TB, BRCA1/2 genotyping, forensic DNA identification, COVID-19 RT-PCR, and prenatal genetic testing all depend on PCR. Hot-start Taq variants (antibody-inhibited) prevent mispriming during setup, improving specificity in clinical assays. High-fidelity variants (Pfu, Phusion, Q5) with proofreading exonucleases are used for cloning and NGS library preparation.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of Taq polymerase Klenow fragment showing the classic 'right-hand' fold: palm (red, catalytic Asp residues), fingers (blue, O-helix), and thumb (green) subdomains. The DNA duplex binding cleft runs between the thumb and palm.

Electrostatic surface of Taq polymerase showing the positively charged DNA-binding cleft (blue) between thumb and palm domains. The dNTP entry site in the fingers domain is flanked by negatively charged residues that coordinate Mg2+ cofactors.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: Taq DNA polymerase Klenow fragment (1S5L) at 2.3 Å—the right-hand fold is the universal architecture of all B-family and A-family DNA polymerases.

panels.caption: Taq polymerase active site showing two catalytic Asp residues (Asp610, Asp785, orange sticks) coordinating two Mg2+ ions (green spheres) for the two-metal-ion mechanism. The O-helix (Tyr671, blue) closes over the incoming dNTP to enforce Watson-Crick base pair geometry.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: Taq polymerase catalytic site—two Mg2+ ions bridged by Asp610 and Asp785 catalyze nucleotidyl transfer; the O-helix enforces Watson-Crick selectivity.

key_facts: Taq polymerase Klenow fragment structure solved at 2.3 Å by Li, Korolev, and Waksman at Washington University, published in Structure in 1998.
Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus (Yellowstone hot springs) is thermostable at 95 degrees C, enabling automated PCR thermocycling.
The right-hand fold (palm, fingers, thumb) is universal among DNA polymerases; the O-helix closes over the dNTP to enforce base-pair fidelity.
Taq lacks 3'-5' proofreading exonuclease, giving an error rate of ~1 per 10,000 nt; high-fidelity variants (Pfu, Phusion, Q5) have proofreading domains.
Kary Mullis received the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for inventing PCR; Taq polymerase made it practical and scalable.
PCR enables HIV/HCV viral load testing, COVID-19 RT-PCR diagnostics, BRCA1/2 cancer risk genotyping, forensic identification, and NGS library preparation.
Hot-start Taq (antibody-inhibited) prevents non-specific amplification during room-temperature setup of clinical PCR assays.
significance: The Taq polymerase structure revealed the mechanistic basis of thermostable DNA replication and PCR fidelity, enabling rational engineering of polymerases with improved accuracy and substrate range for next-generation sequencing and diagnostics. PCR, the technology Taq enables, has become the indispensable tool of modern medicine: it diagnoses infectious diseases, guides cancer therapy, enables forensic identification, and underpins the genomics revolution.

name: p53 DNA-Binding Domain
title: The Guardian of the Genome: p53 and the Structural Basis of Cancer's Most Mutated Gene
abstract: The p53 tumor suppressor is mutated in over 50% of all human cancers. Yung-Chi Cho, Stephen Gorina, Paul Jeffrey, and Nikola Pavletich solved the 2.2 Å crystal structure of the p53 DNA-binding domain in complex with its DNA response element in 1994 at Memorial Sloan Kettering, revealing how the zinc-coordinated beta-sandwich scaffold positions the loop-sheet-helix motif for sequence-specific DNA recognition.

sections.content: The Most Important Tumor Suppressor

In 1994, Yung-Chi Cho, Stephen Gorina, Paul D. Jeffrey, and Nikola P. Pavletich at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center published the 2.2 Å crystal structure of the p53 DNA-binding domain (DBD) in complex with its DNA consensus sequence in Science. p53 is activated by DNA damage, oncogene activation, and hypoxia; it induces cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, or apoptosis. Over 50% of human tumors carry p53 mutations, making it the most commonly mutated gene in cancer.
See Fig. 1
Zinc-Coordinated Core and DNA Contacts

The p53 DBD adopts a beta-sandwich scaffold that serves as the stable platform for the DNA-binding surface. A zinc ion coordinated by Cys176, His179, Cys238, and Cys242 is essential for structural integrity; zinc loss upon mutation destabilizes the domain. Three structural elements contact DNA: the loop-sheet-helix motif inserts Arg248 into the DNA minor groove (the most common mutation site in cancer); Arg273 and Ala276 contact the DNA backbone phosphates in the major groove.
See Fig. 2
Cancer Mutations and Drug Restoration

Six hotspot mutations (R175H, G245S, R248W, R248Q, R249S, R273H, R273C, R282W) account for ~30% of all p53 cancer mutations. Structural analysis shows these mutations either destabilize the beta-sandwich (structural mutants: R175H, R249S) or directly eliminate DNA contact residues (contact mutants: R248W, R273H). APR-246 (Eprenetapopt) restores wild-type conformation to structural p53 mutants and received FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation for myelodysplastic syndrome with mutant p53.

panels.caption: Ribbon diagram of p53 DNA-binding domain (blue) in complex with the DNA response element half-site (orange). The beta-sandwich core (yellow) supports the loop-sheet-helix motif contacting DNA major and minor grooves. The zinc ion (green sphere) at the L2/L3 interface is visible.

Electrostatic surface of p53 DBD showing the positively charged DNA-binding face (blue) contacting the electronegative DNA backbone (red). The minor groove-inserting L3 loop region is the most electropositive area.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 1: p53 DNA-binding domain (1TUP) at 2.2 Å in complex with its DNA response element—the beta-sandwich scaffold and zinc coordination site are clearly resolved.

panels.caption: p53 DNA interface showing key contacts: Arg248 (orange) inserted into the DNA minor groove (most frequently mutated cancer residue), Arg273 (blue) contacting the DNA backbone phosphate in the major groove, and Zn2+ (green sphere) coordinated by Cys176, His179, Cys238, Cys242.

figure_plan.overall_caption: Fig. 2: p53 cancer hotspot residues at the DNA interface—Arg248 (R248W/Q) inserts into the minor groove; Arg273 (R273H/C) contacts phosphates. Both mutations eliminate DNA binding while leaving the overall fold intact.

key_facts: p53 DNA-binding domain complex solved at 2.2 Å by Cho, Gorina, Jeffrey, and Pavletich at MSKCC, published in Science in 1994.
p53 is mutated in >50% of human cancers, making it the most commonly altered gene in all of oncology.
The beta-sandwich scaffold is stabilized by a Zn2+ ion (Cys176/His179/Cys238/Cys242); zinc loss destabilizes structural mutants like R175H.
Six hotspot residues (R175, G245, R248, R249, R273, R282) account for ~30% of all p53 cancer mutations.
Arg248 is the single most mutated residue in cancer; in wild-type structure it inserts into the DNA minor groove at the CATG tetrad of the response element.
APR-246 (Eprenetapopt) restores wild-type conformation to structural p53 mutants; received FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation.
p53 activates transcription of over 100 target genes involved in cell cycle arrest (p21), apoptosis (PUMA, NOXA), and DNA repair (GADD45).
significance: The p53 structure explained the molecular basis of the most important tumor suppressor in human biology and directly revealed why specific hotspot mutations cause cancer by disrupting DNA recognition. This structural knowledge has driven 30 years of drug discovery targeting mutant p53 reactivation, culminating in clinical-stage compounds that restore p53 function in cancer cells. The structure remains the central reference for interpreting newly discovered p53 mutations in cancer genomes.
